First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $\frac{9\pi }{2}$ that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9\pi }{2}-2\pi  & =\frac{5\pi }{2} \\ \frac{5\pi }{2}-2\pi  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{2}).$

The angle ${90}^{∘}$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14253609/assets/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}=\frac{0}{1}=0.
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{2})=0.$
